title: Section 482: Saving of Inherent Power of High Court
facts: Section 482 CrPC recognizes the inherent power of the High Court to pass orders for justice.
It is usually invoked in cases of malicious prosecution, quashing of FIRs, and prevention of abuse of process.
The power is used where the lower court's proceedings are fundamentally flawed or when justice cannot be secured otherwise.
issues: Whether the High Court should intervene in a case where a trial is ongoing.
The conditions under which an FIR or criminal complaint can be quashed.
The distinction between Section 482 (inherent power) and Section 397 (revisional power).
analysis_of_law: Inherent Power: It is a non-exhaustible power of the High Court to check abuse of judicial process.
Scope: To give effect to any order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, or to secure the ends of justice.
Constraint: It should be exercised sparingly, carefully, and with caution (ex debito justitiae).
precedent_analysis: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal: Laid down 7 categories of cases where FIR/proceedings can be quashed under Section 482.

Gian Singh v. State of Punjab: Held that for cases which are predominantly civil (commercial, family, matrimonial), proceedings can be quashed even for non-compoundable offenses if settlement is reached.
courts_reasoning: Justice is the ultimate goal of the legal code. Section 482 is the 'valve' that prevents injustice when the rigid adherence to standard procedure would lead to absurdity.
One cannot allow a criminal trial to become an instrument of harassment when no case exists on the face of the record.
High Courts must ensure that the accused is not subjected to an unnecessary and vexatious trial.
conclusion: Section 482 is a vital safeguard in the Indian criminal justice system.
It remains a powerful remedy for individuals facing meritless criminal litigation.
full_ratio: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC is vast and designed to ensure justice is done and the court process is not abused. It can be used to quash FIRs and criminal trials if the allegations are vexatious, baseless, or if the dispute is predominantly civil and has been settled.
